subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CANADIAN DELEGATION TO MEETING OF PREPARATORY COMMISSION

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):	Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house of the composition of the Canadian delegation to the preparatory commission of the united nations organization, which will meet in London on November 23.

United Nations-Preparatory Commission
Following the pattern adopted for the delegation to the San Francisco conference-and I think I can say that it is felt on both sides of the house that this was a very successful pattern-the government has decided to appoint a delegation representative of both houses of parliament and of both sides of this house. The chairman of the delegation will be Mr. L. D. Wilgress, Canadian Ambassador in Moscow, who attended the San Francisco conference as an alternate delegate. The parliamentary members of the delegation will be the Hon. A. K. Hugessen, from the senate; the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Winkler); the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), who was a delegate at San Francisco; the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard), and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). These six gentlemen will be the Canadian delegates. The list of advisers to the delegation will be announced later.
The charter of the united nations was unanimously approved by both houses of parliament, and we are naturally anxious to ensure continued general support from all Canadians in taking the further steps which are necessary to bring the united nations organization into active operation. The work to be done by the preparatory commission is not so dramatic as that which was accomplished at San Francisco. It is, nevertheless, of great importance towards ensuring the smooth and efficient operation of the general assembly, the security council, the social and economic council, the secretariat and the other parts of the united nations organization. During September and October the executive committee of the preparatory commission has been very busily occupied in London preparing recommendations for the consideration of the full commission at its forthcoming session. These recommendations deal with a great variety of subjects, many of them of a technical character. Canada has been represented on the executive committee by the Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon, Canadian Ambassador in Brussels, with assistants from the Department of External Affairs.
It is hoped that the preparatory commission will complete its work in about three weeks, and that the first session of the general assembly of the united nations may be convened shortly after the New Year. The present intention is that this session of the assembly should be divided into two parts. The first part would be concerned with the adoption of regulations placed before it by the preparatory commission, elections to the various other organizations of the united nations, the appointment of the secretary-general, the provision of the necessary means
of financing and cognate matters relating to organization. The plan is that the assembly would then adjourn so that the security council, the social and economic council and the secretary-general could establish themselves in action and the assembly would then meet for the second part of its first session after an interval of some months, in order to discharge the high functions vested in it by the charter.

MUTUAL AID-SUPPLIES NOT LOADED ON SHIPS ON V-E AND V-J DAYS
speechtext:
1.	(a) On V-E day and (b) on V-J day, were there any mutual aid supplies which had not been loaded on ships?
2.	If so, (a) did the government repossess such supplies, (b) when?
3.	(a) What were such supplies; (b) what countries were notified that the government had repossessed such supplies; (c) for how long did the government retain its title to such supplies? .

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: MUTUAL AID-SUPPLIES NOT LOADED ON SHIPS ON V-E AND V-J DAYS
speechtext:
1.	(a) Yes; (b) yes.
2.	(a and b) Goods which had not been loaded aboard a vessel as at midnight, September 1, were retained as the property of the Canadian government, and countries receiving goods after that date were requested to pay for them, and received them on condition that they undertake to do so. An exception was made in the case of certain minesweepers which
Canada had explicitly undertaken in advance to provide as mutual aid to the U.S.S.R. notwithstanding the end of hostilities.
3.	(a) Inventories of a large number of supplies which had been ordered by the mutual aid board were on hand, in transit, in storage, and in the course of manufacture at the conclusion of hostilities. Detailed inventories have not yet been compiled but some indication of the nature of the goods in question can be obtained by noting, in the reports of the mutual aid board, the types of goods being supplied as mutual aid. It is known however, that large numbers of aircraft, automotive equipment and spares, ordnance equipment, unfinished ships, and radio equipment were included, as well as food stuffs.
(b)	All countries receiving mutual aid were notified or told that following the end of hostilities they would be expected to pay for supplies received from Canada. In general, mutual aid supplies were not transferred until loaded on ship; consequently repossession of supplies already transferred was confined to certain items being held in depots in Canada for the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom authorities have been notified that Canada regards these supplies as having reverted to Canadian ownership in accordance with the mutual aid agreement.
(c)	Title to the supplies in question has been retained until favourable opportunities for sale of them have occurred. Items of civilian types, such as food stuffs, were generally sold immediately to the countries for which they had been destined as mutual aid. Items remaining as surplus are being declared as such and turned over to War Assets Corporation for disposal,

speechtext: With regard to this motion, I would point out to the house that it calls for the production of reports from an investigator to his superior officer-a chief investigator-and for the same reasons on account of which reports of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to their superiors, and officials of that character throughout the whole public service, have always been regarded as privileged, I must take the position that these reports are privileged and that it is not in the public interest for them to be produced. maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO ASSIST MR. SPEAKER IN REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to object in part to the text with regard * to this particular proceeding at the present time, for the appointment of the committee. May I have it understood that while I am in favour of appointing the committee, I am not in favour of its appointment along some of the lines indicated.
On the last occasion this matter was before the house there was an extended debate on the subject. A committee was appointed, and a report was brought down. I was sorry that that report was not adopted.
For a few moments may I revert to our proceedings, which to a great extent are bound up with the rules which obtain in the British House of Commons. Ad Westminster much has been done to shorten proceedings, and to a great extent this has been brought about by the question period extending for three quarters of an hour from 2.45 p.m. to 3.30 p.m. each day.
A new book on parliamentary procedure was published in 1930 by G. F. M. Campion, second clerk assistant of the British House of Commons. He has been knighted and is now Clerk of the House. I may point out that our present rules are sufficiently broad to enable the asking of supplementary questions when the orders of the day are called, He states:
Not later than three o'clock the question "hour" begins. This is a more important item of business than any yet described. It is expected to provide lively moments and seems to be of unfailing interest to members and the public. It is modern and affords a useful method of supervising the administration of the government. Its effectiveness is generally recognized. Questions "turn a searchlight upon every corner of the public service." (Lowell,
Revision of Rules

i. 332.) Their chief object is "the explanation to the public of the meaning of political events", and "they are -often arranged by the government itself, so as to give them an opportunity of making announcements in a somewhat information way." (Redlich, ii. 241 and 242.) They are "serviceable as obviating the necessity in many instances of more extended debate and of motions for papers." (Todd, 1982, ii 85.) And finally, "Questions afford to the private member under modern conditions almost his only opportunity." (Marriott, i. 571.)
It will be noted that under our standing orders, in all cases not provided for in our rules the usages and customs of the British House of Commons as in force at the time shall be followed. I am quite certain that it is a member's right to ask any pertinent question of a minister, on the orders of the day being called, and Mr. Speaker could not prevent the adoption of that practice in this house. I believe we do not need any amendment to our rules to enable the asking of supplementary questions. In my view our rules are broad enough to permit that, but it should be made very plain in our new rules if questions are short.
When the committee is appointed I hope something will be done along these lines, because I believe if we are allowed to ask questions when the orders of the day are called it will expedite proceedings, and eliminate a great deal'of debate. I have here the British Hansard of August 23 in which I find that a large number of questions were asked in the British house on the orders of the day, seventy-five per cent of which questions would be ruled out of order here. This committee is being appointed and should at once consider the privileges of private members of the house, which are being taken away. We had an example of that to-day.
In conclusion, I should like to pay a tribute to your predecessors as speakers and yourself, and' especially to the very learned Clerk of the House of Commons who has devoted his whole life to the public service and who is without a peer for efficiency, fair dealing, kindness and courtesy. I think such a tribute is long overdue to him from all sections of the house for the able way in which he has helped the house with dignity to transact its business.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am entirely in accord with the motion to appoint a committee to consider changes in the rules and to make recommendations accordingly to the house. That such changes are necessary seems to be evidenced from what has happened to me within the last week in this house. I do not know that that requires a change in the rules so much as living up to the rules.

A few days ago the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) used certain words of which I complained as being offensive as applied to me. He said:
It was a malicious and wicked attempt to deprecate the province of Quebec in the minds of the people of our sister provinces.
The house was in committee of the whole at the time, with the Deputy Speaker in the chair. It will be observed that on November 1 when acting as chairman the Deputy Speaker ruled that it was too late for me then to ask the hon. member for Temiscouata to withdraw his statement, and he did so on the authority of section 261, page 107, of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, which reads:
The proper time for interference is when the offensive expressions are uttered, and not afterwards; and it may take place, either on the Speaker's voluntary motion, or on the call to order of the member assailed, or of some other member, or the general call of the house.
He stopped there, but the following paragraph is equally, perhaps more important. It reads as follows-

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO ASSIST MR. SPEAKER IN REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Order. I would call the attention of hon. members to paragraph 118, page 35, of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, which reads:
Silence is required to be observed in both houses. In the Commons, all members should be silent, or should converse only in whispers.

maintopic: SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO ASSIST MR. SPEAKER IN REVISION OF STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Now I shall have less difficulty in being heard. The part of section 261 which the Deputy Speaker failed to read is as follows-I quote from page 108 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition:
The Speaker feels more strongly his duty to interpose and check language which seems unparliamentary with regard to an absent member.
When the words were used by the hon. member for Temiscouata as applied to me I was not in the chamber, and therefore it was the duty of the Deputy Speaker, who was in the chair, to take the necessary steps to see that the member who used those offensive words withdrew them. But he did not do so, and therefore, Mr. Speaker, I maintain that there was a dereliction of duty on his part, and I hope that when this committee meets it will revise the rules so as to provide a suitable punishment for such an offence.
I should like to call attention to another paragraph in Beauchesne which applies with equal force to what happened on that occasion. Paragraph 231 on page 98 reads:
If offensive words are spoken in committee, which are taken down, the house only, and not the committee, can take notice of them.

subtopic: PRIZE COURTS AND PRIZE LAW-EXCHEQUER COURT JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Section 1, I assume, affords an opportunity for certain general references which I should like to make at this stage.
So- far as the legislation as a whole is concerned, the purpose of the bill is to invest jurisdiction in prize matters in the Exchequer Court of Canada and to provide certain rules governing the exercise of jurisdiction. Prior to 1934, when the Canadian Admiralty Act was passed, the exchequer court bad this jurisdiction. During recent years there has been a very great increase in the number of cases in the exchequer court, with the result that the exchequer court as at present constituted is unable properly to discharge its responsibilities. The growth of litigation in the exchequer court has been phenomenal since the outbreak of war by reason of the fact that so many crown corporations have been set up; and the situation for litigants in that court is becoming intolerable. All interested in the administration of justice are agreed in this, that one of the first qualifications of a court is that justice should be assured; and the second principle, which is of equal importance, is that justice should be made expeditious. And yet, with three judges on the exchequer coutt, all of them most estimable men, the situation is such that something must be done in order to assure a greater degree of expedition than has prevailed since the outbreak of the war. When I say that to-day there are 100 judgments on cases that have been argued in the Exchequer Court of Canada and that are more than one year overdue, some indication is given of the pile-up of work and the necessity for something being done to assure greater expedition in the handing down of these judgments.

The matter came about in this way. There was an arrangement entered into in 1944, of which we were apprised, between the allies, that there would be no prize salvage as between them. Prize salvage is the recompense for retaking from the enemy something belonging to ourselves or to an ally that had been captured by the enemy; and it was suggested that we make it a provision that no prize salvage proceedings could be instituted without the consent of the Attorney General. That was done by an order in council. When the matter was brought to my attention I suggested at once that we have this dealt with immediately by order in council, because it was urgent, but that we have a bill prepared providing for prize court jurisdiction otherwise than by order in council; that we have it by statute. That statute was prepared, but at the following sessions there was no opportunity to have it dealt with because of the pressure of war legislation which was more urgently required, and the bill now before the committee is for the purpose of setting up a prize court by statute under conditions which conform with the arrangements we have had since the beginning of the war with the United Kingdom and our other allies.

I had asked the law officers to try to codify that law, but they told me that much of it wTas in archaic language that had been construed by court decisions, and that it would be extremely difficult and somewhat risky to attempt to express it in the terms of a statute; that if we wished to make no change which might be prejudicial to some interest the thing to do was to take that law as it existed and leave to the courts the responsibility of determining judicially, from the statutes, from the decisions of the courts and from their knowledge of international law, what were the rights arising out of the capture of prize as an act of war. subtopic: PRIZE COURTS AND PRIZE LAW-EXCHEQUER COURT JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Before they were instituted was it necessary to obtain the permission of the Attorney General?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. At that time there was no requirement for permission of the Attorney General. In 1864 a United Kingdom statute was adopted which formed part of the prize law and which provided that:
Where any ship or goods belonging to any of his majesty's subjects after being taken as prize by the enemy is or are retaken from the enemy by any of his majesty's ships of war, the same shall be restored by a decree of a prize court to the owner on his paying a prize salvage one-eighth part of the value of the prize, to be decreed as ascertained by the court, or such sum not exceeding one-eighth part of the unestimated value of the prize as may be agreed upon between the owner and the recaptors, and approved by order of the court: provided that where the recapture is made under circumstances of similar difficulty or danger the prize court, if it thinks fit, award to the re-captors as prize salvage a larger part than one-eighth part but not exceeding in any case one-fourth part of the value .of the prize: provided also that, where a ship after being so taken is set forth or used by any of his majesty's enemies as a ship of war, this provision for restitution shall not apply, and the ship shall be adjudicated on as in other cases of prize.
It was because of the existence of that statute and because of an understanding arrived at between the allies that there would not be prize salvage as between them that a bill was introduced into the British parliament in March, 1944, determining that no proceedings to enforce a claim for services rendered in retaking a ship, aircraft or goods taken by an enemy shall be instituted after the passing of this act wdthout the consent of the admiralty or the secretary of state.
It was suggested to us that we pass similar legislation. As we had no statutory legislation

with respect to a prize court, I felt at the time that it would be inappropriate to limit by statute a jurisdiction which existed merely under order in council, so I asked at the time that a bill be prepared to create by statute a prize court; to include in that bill the provision asked for by the United Kingdom authorities to carry out their undertaking; and to provide for carrying out that undertaking in the meantime by a further order in council. That is what was done, and' that is one of the orders in council which I cited in my opening remarks on the second reading of the bill.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, that would be going beyond what is provided by the restriction as it is contained in section 6. The restriction in that section is not to apply to prizes, but rather to prize salvage. Prize salvage was a recompense for retaking from the enemy something which the enemy had captured. That was the only thing covered by the arrangement among the allies.

And it was for the purpose of allowing such a claim to be made only with the consent of the admiralty or the secretary of state that the bill to which I have referred was introduced in the parliament of the United Kingdom. I state this only as an explanation of the chronological development.
At the outbreak of the war we had no prize court, and provided for one by order in council. Then it was suggested to us that we alter the situation by statute. I felt, rightly or wrongly, that it would not be proper to ask parliament by statute to impose a restriction upon what had been done by order in council. We felt when we came before parliament we should ask it to deal with the whole question, and in the meantime we would implement this undertaking to the allies by means of further restrictive orders in council under the War Measures Act.

This will possibly
give an opportunity to discuss this question of the fiat or order of the Attorney General permitting the taking of an action. This is a matter which has been dealt with on a number of occasions by the Canadian Bar association, the feeling generally being this, that having regard to the diversity of activity in which the government participates to-day, and having regard to the expansion of the activities of the government, the doctrine upon which the issue of a fiat is based should no longer be in effect. That generally is the viewpoint, I believe, expressed by committees of the Canadian Bar association which have dealt with this particular matter; and I feel that a statement by the Minister of Justice on this question would be very much welcomed. The procedure is based, no doubt,
upon the principle that "the king can do no wrong", and that therefore the king should not be brought before the courts of the land. I realize and I think the bar generally does, that under the present Minister of Justice there has been a considerable widening of the issue of fiats. I can think of one series of cases which came up some years ago, started by the Indians in Saskatchewan as against the Indian department for an accounting. A fiat was granted in one case. That case came before the exchequer court. It revealed that the Indians were receiving treatment which was far from what it should be, and that considerable sums of money rightfully belonging to this tribe of Indians should be returned to it. From that date on, other Indian tribes endeavouring to get fiats found themselves unable to get them.
I think that, generally speaking, the people of Canada believe that the time has come when this ancient doctrine of the inability of the subject excepting with the consent of the crown, to sue the crown should be, if not altogether removed, certainly diminished so as to enable justice to be done as between the subject and His Majesty the King.

subtopic: PRIZE COURTS AND PRIZE LAW-EXCHEQUER COURT JURISDICTION
speechtext:
There is just an additional word which might be said on that topic, that it never takes very long to know what the Department of Justice will do. I think requests for fiats are received there and dealt *with the day they are received. But the antiquated practice requires, or at least it did when I knew more of the Department of Justice than I do now, that the fiat go to the department affected, and there it has to wait until somebody dies or somebody blasts it out of the baskets of gentlemen who have things that they consider more important to do than to consider why their department should be pursued before the courts, and why gentlemen's peace and equanimity should be disturbed by being haled before the tribunals of the land to explain something they cannot explain.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: With respect to the question of petitions of right, I am not in a position at this time to state any other government policy than that of respect for the traditional prerogatives of the crown.
The matter has been frequently under discussion. There were reports required from the interested departments every time a petition of right was filed, and sometimes those reports took a very long time in coming back. For a considerable time now I have asked the officers, when sending out a request for information, to inform the department
Canada Prize Act

that the petition had been received and that a recommendation for a fiat would be made at the expiry of thirty days unless in the meantime they submitted good reasons for doing otherwise. I believe that method has speeded up considerably the issuing of fiats.

subtopic: PRIZE COURTS AND PRIZE LAW-EXCHEQUER COURT JURISDICTION
speechtext: On the question of traditions of right to which the minister referred a moment ago, it seems to me there is much merit in what my hon. friend the member for Lake Centre has said, and for a reason which appeals to me and will, I think, appeal to the committee generally. Year by year, owing to the trend of conditions in Canada, and perhaps elsewhere, government departments are dealing in a business way with more of the citizens than they have since confederation. This means, of course, that determinations of rights as between the various departments of government and the individuals with whom they deal have become much more multitudinous, and the business, of course, has become much more important than it was in those days when the idea existed that there was reluctance on the part of governments to grant fiats. I believe the minister should carefully consider the whole question of the granting of fiats in the light of changed1 conditions, which are not simply a matter of argument and theory, but are actually established facts under the present circumstances of government operation. For one individual who in former days would have business dealings with the government, there are to-day, I suppose, twenty-five; perhaps even that does not present the picture in an unduly exaggerated form. That being the case, it seems to me that there is a special reason and a powerful argument for the widening of powers with respect to the giving of fiats. It is an easy thing to deny an individual his rights when he is dealing with a government under the present system. Too much power, if I may say so, rests in the department which would be, in the event of litigation, a party to the suit. That is something which the minister might carefully review in the light of the changed conditions I have just described.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION

speechtext: Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National War Services) moved the second reading of bill No. 13, to amend the War Charities Act, 1939.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext: Does the minister intend to say something about the bill at this stage?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
The purpose of these
amendments is to bring all types of war memorial appeals under the purview of the War Charities Act. I may say that certain influential bodies throughout the country have made representations to the department that in their judgment it would be advisable if the war charities administration included the supervision of funds for war memorials. The Canadian chamber of commerce have made inquiries whether or not certain rules or procedures could be established for war memorial funds such as are now registered under the War Charities Act. There would be another advantage in having war memorial funds come within the jurisdiction of the War Charities Act, and it would mean that certain charitable organizations that would be approved by the department could automatically be accepted by the income tax division for purposes of the Income War Tax Act.
The main amendments to the act are amendments to section 1, and that extends the present definition of war charity fund to include appeals for war memorials. A new paragraph (c) has been added to define war memorial for the purposes of the act, and as will be noted in the bill which is now before the committee, war memorial shall include:
-any building or other structure erected, constructed, acquired, developed or maintained, or

War Charities Act
any real property acquired to commemorate the war or to preserve the memory of those who served in the war that has been either before or after erection, construction, acquisition, development, or the commencement of the maintenance designated by' regulation as a war memorial or is of a class that has been designated by regulation as a class of war memorials.
The War Charities Act has operated very efficiently during the six years of conflict, and the administration of the act has enjoyed the confidence of the Canadian public to a very marked degree. It has assured careful custodianship of public contributions averaging $30,000,000 annually for war charity purposes. It has also assured that these funds were raised at very low expense, that no personal profit accrued to the promoters, and that funds were put to useful purposes without duplication of services.
I am sure it will be of interest to the committee to learn that some four thousand funds and branches have held registration under the act at one time or another throughout the war years, and at September 30, 1945, the registration stood at 3,611. The termination of the war is bringing about a decline in the registration for truly war purposes, but an increase in registrations for rehabilitation piu-poses, and the department has been receiving many applications from war service funds throughout the country that these funds be transferred to other people or to other funds or organizations for the purpose of instituting some type of war memorial in these several communities.
May I say that these amendments to the act are purely for the purpose of protecting the public and seeing that the money which will be in those funds is handled properly and properly accounted for. I do not know that there is any further explanation I can give at this particular time, but when the amendments are under discussion I shall be glad to answer such questions as may be asked.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
I think we can welcome this bill, and for several reasons. One of them is that it recognizes the trend across Canada in the choosing of war memorials. Generally speaking throughout Canada to-day there is a disposition to get away from the idea of erecting blocks of stone as the only memorials to those who served this country in the war, and of trying to select memorials which will be not only ornamental but useful to the men who return and to their children and the children and relatives of those who lost their lives in our country's service.
I think in that particular the amendments to the act which are now proposed are to be
commended. I believe too that the statement of the minister that an act of this description is being placed before the house in order to protect the public is one which will receive general approval from this house. I may add too that I believe the action of parliament in p'assing the War Charities Act several years ago was a protection to the public during the war from anything that might have savoured otherwise of fraud or of the mismanagement of funds that were meant to be used for specific purposes. There may have been abuses, but I do not know of them.
I believe that parliament acted wisely when it passed legislation making it necessary to obtain the approval of the department of funds to be raised during the war for charitable purposes. If we take the old definition of the word "charity" I think the term is all right. But if we think of the colloquial interpretation of the word "charity", it is all wrong when used in this connection. But I take it that this is following the old usage; and that in this case charity means a token of love rather than the relief of poverty and need. Therefore I want to say that we are generally in favour of this legislation.
I do not know just how liberal the interpretation of war memorials will be. That will depend very largely on the administration of the act and on the interpretation of the terms to be found in it. If the interpretations are to be made in the manner in which the language indicates, we shall have a pretty broad interpretation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
The intention is to make
it as broad as possible.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
That is what I should
think, from the language of the bill itself. I know that in many parts of Canada there are projects under way now -for the establishment in small towns, of memorial parks, community centres, community hospitals, libraries, and the like. They, I think, commend themselves not only to the men who are returning to those communities, from overseas, but to those whose sacrifices these memorials are intended to remember. The greater the extent to which we can work out a plan of encouraging provinces, municipalities and local communities to set up memorials which will be of use to the present generation and to posterity, the more effective those memorials will be.
In the interpretation of the bill I hope that some consideration may be given to something of which I have some knowledge, where a small town, with a relatively small assessment, desires to embark upon a memorial scheme which will benefit the people not only of the
War Charities Act

town itself but of the whole adjacent community, and yet the adjacent community may not be in a position to levy a tax on itself for a project somewhere else, we will say, in the adjacent town, or may even find it very difficult to do so, or perhaps even to get by some of the local government boards which have the supervision of such matters. I hope that there will- be a combination of the two, that such a town or village may embark upon a fairly substantial project, and may come under this measure so that they may appeal to the people of the neighbourhood with a view to using, by way of voluntary contribution as well as by taxation, an amount over and above that which can be raised in the ordinary way in the local village or town.
I am keenly interested, as I think we all are, in making provisions particularly in our smaller towns and rural communities, for re. creation facilities for our young people. When we read the delinquency statistics across this country to-day I think we must be filled with alarm at the amount of delinquency in the teen-age groups and those a little older. I am of the opinion that this is largely because we have not provided sufficient recreational facilities for the adolescent youth of our country.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
There are many delinquent
parents in these days.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
I know. I agree with
the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) that some of this stems from delinquent parents. I am not suggesting it is not so; it is so. On the other hand if the delinquency of parents can be mitigated in some degree by having the right kind of community activity to take care of the children who are neglected by their parents, and particularly the younger group of people, we shall have achieved a great deal. I am referring particularly to people in adolescence or early manhood and womanhood who have energies which can be used for good or ill. By providing recreational facilities of the right sort we not only develop the physique; I think-[DOT] and I am now speaking as one who for a long time was engaged in directing the studies of youth-that proceeding in the right way in this regard we can do a great deal for both the physical and the moral development of these young people.
Even in a city like Ottawa-and the same applies to larger cities-there are not enough facilities of this kind. We are considering the beautifying of the city as a national memorial, but at the same time we must give a good deal of attention to the recreation facilities that are to be established even in a city like Ottawa. If that may be said of Ottawa, it

may be said with much more force of some places remote -from Ottawa where even the facilities that we have here are inadequate.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext: It is true right across the country.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext: Yes. I say even in this capital city, where we have some of these things, we need more facilities of this sort. I think if the men who have sacrified their lives in this war could come back and choose the type of memorial they would prefer, having in mind1 their own youthful experiences in this country this is the sort of thing they would approve rather than merely some piece of stone which may be, in a way, only a passing memory.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext: It does not enthuse.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
No; it is only a passing memory. We of this generation who read the names of those who perished in the war perhaps will be reminded1 from time to time of some young men with whom we have associated, some we have known and respected and for whom we have had affection, but to future generations they will be just names. On the other hand the results of the building up of the physique and the moral fibre of our youth are passed on from generation to generation, and I think make for the greatest contribution to our nation. So I am very glad indeed to be able to rise and express these views, not only on my own behalf and in behalf of those associated with me but I believe in behalf of a good many people across this country; and I hope advantage may be taken of this act in many communities.
- I know some communities already have endeavoured to do something in this regard. I seldom advertise my own constituency in this house, because I think that is not what I am here for; but when I was out in my own constituency in the summer I found that in the small towrn of Rosetown, with a population according to the last census of some 1,400 people, speaking from memory, they had engaged a veteran, a young airman, to whom they were paying $2,000 a year to organize recreation in that progressive little town and for the community surrounding it, and already the results could be seen after even a very few months. I think if we could encourage similar efforts in the small towns as well as in a larger way across the country it would contribute to what we are all interested in, the building up of a better manhood and womanhood in the country in which we live.


War Charities Act

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the bill. I wish to say also that while I agree with much of what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said, I think this idea of memorial parks may be played to a bit of an extreme. My view is that parks and playgrounds and recreational centres are positively the duty and business of governments anyway, regardless of memorials. These are things we should have, the things we all want, the things for which we are all pressing. Every community and every small town in the country would like something of that kind. I live in a very small village where there is practically no recreation for the children and young people except a few swings in the corner of a lot which has been fenced off by the town fathers. If they want a swimming pool, some club such as the Lion's club or some other organization comes along and initiates a movement for that purpose. If you say, "Well, why was this not done a long time ago?" naturally the communities reply, "We haven't any money." It is always the same old story. But my answer is that in a civilization such as we think we have, in any case, those things should be done quite apart from the question of memorials.
I am not altogether in sympathy with the idea that a monument is just a block of stone. Perhaps it is bordering on the sentimental and ejpotional side to think of a memorial of stone as representing the graves of those who may be buried in other parts of the world, but if you took sentiment and emotion out of life we would live in a pretty cold sort of civilization. I think of the memorial down here on the plaza. I know it cost a great deal of money, but I am rather proud of that memorial when I walk by it. Not only do I see its magnificance; I think to myself that it represents something, just the same. I do not believe I have ever passed that memorial and noticed a wreath, for instance, which somebody has put there, without thinking in my heart, "Well, some mother or some wife has done that in honour of her lost loved one." I am reminded of a beautiful little park in the city of Calgary. It is called Central park; it is only about a block long, but they take particularly good care of it. I want to compliment the government on its choice of the properties now housing the Belcher hospital, which is right across the road from this beautiful little park. Just between the soldiers' hospital and the end of the park, in the park grounds, is a fine modern type of stone memorial to those who gave their lives in the last war, and there are places where people can sit down. I have passed
there many times when soldiers have been sitting about; often I have seen wreaths on that monument. Many of our soldiers and airmen are missing; they just have not turned up. In some instances the mothers and fathers of those boys just do not know where they lie to-night; they do not know where they are buried. That is my case; I do not know where my son is buried. You may call it sentiment if you like. We go to the graves of those buried in our cemeteries, perhaps on their birthdays or on the anniversary of their death, and we put flowers on their graves. Well, there are some citizens in Canada who cannot do that; but they can place flowers on a suitable memorial.
I am not saying that funds should not be granted for parks and recreational centres in honour of our fighting men. I am quite certain they would enjoy libraries and things like that, but let us not go to the other extreme. Let us have our parks. Let us have good parks. Let us have them well kept, even though it does cost money, and in those parks let us have suitable memorials as well, even though they are of stone, because even stone can sometimes speak.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the two previous speakers that within the next few years a great many memorials will be erected in honour of those who lost their lives in the last war, and I believe the policy outlined in this bill is one which should commend itself to all hon. members of this house.
I was greatly interested in the statement of the minister as to the amount of money that [DOT] had been collected by charitable organizations. I must say I believe that the regulations made in 1939, ensuring that these moneys would be properly held and properly expended, effected a very good purpose. The reason for this amendment is to ensure that it will not be a matter of collecting money and handing it over, but rather one of erecting something that will be permanent.
Hon. members who have preceded me spoke about municipalities. As I understand it, municipalities have their powers given them by the laws of the provinces. I know that is the position in Ontario. In that province a year or two ago legislation somewhat similar to this was enacted, under which the province gave to the municipalities-cities, towns, villages, townships, counties, as the case may be-power to do what this measure allows private organizations to do. I take it that in many instances municipalities will be erecting
War Charities Act

memorials, and as municipalities are corporations with long or everlasting life, they will be in a position to maintain those memorials.
It is altogether likely that other more or less permanent institutions, such as those connected with education-whether they be public schools, eollegiates, universities or private schools-will be erecting memorials. No doubt they will be able to maintain them. Church and fraternal organizations will be doing the same, but I am not sure to what extent the educational, church and fraternal organizations will come under this measure. It may be that they will-and if so, I believe it would be in their best interests. Perhaps we should have some explanation or clarification of that point.
As I see it, the great problem is that a number of private organizations will undertake the erection of memorials, and I suggest that something be put in the bill to ensure that memorials erected by these organizations shall be maintained for all time-because there is nothing worse than to see a building, a park or any other memorial fall into a state of decay or disrepair, with no one available to look after it. When we go into committee I shall have something to say on the respective sections.
I suggest that either in this measure, or under the Income War Tax Act, contributions made or funds set aside for the erection of memorials should be considered as charities. It may be that such is the regulation now, although I am not sure.
I believe all members of the opposition are convinced that this is a good measure. We approve the principle, and we shall have something to say when the sections of the bill are considered in committee.

subtopic: INCLUSION OP WAR MEMORIALS AS PROJECTS ACCEPTABLE FOR REGISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have one moment?-atid I promise not to go beyond six o'clock. I am very anxious to say one thing to the minister who is in charge of war memorials, and it is this, that the government or parliament should not spend any of these millions on the national war memorial here until the city of Ottawa spends at least a dollar and a. half to put some names on its own streets. I have hunted this town for six weeks; I have watched very carefully, and I have found only four signs- and they no doubt were put there by the gentleman who originated the great art of camouflage we have heard so much about during the last two years.
On motion of Mr. MacNicol the debate was adjourned.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
